implementation_notes: Java has no generator statement; the standard library supplies lazy production instead. Stream.generate(Supplier) yields an unbounded sequence, Stream.iterate(seed, UnaryOperator) yields seed, f(seed), f(f(seed)) and so on, and the Java 9 overload iterate(seed, hasNext, next) terminates lazily - all driven by the terminal operation, so only the elements the consumer asks for are computed. Reach for a hand-written Iterator (variant) when production owns a closeable resource, a checked exception or state that stream operators cannot express.
code_sketch:
Stream<BigInteger> fibs =
    Stream.iterate(new BigInteger[]{ONE, ONE},
                   p -> new BigInteger[]{p[1], p[0].add(p[1])})
          .map(p -> p[0]);                 // lazy: nothing has run yet

fibs.limit(10).forEach(System.out::println);
pitfalls: Streams are single-use: passing the Stream object around and consuming it twice throws IllegalStateException, so store the factory (or a Supplier<Stream<T>>), not the stream.

Laziness ends at the terminal operation: without limit/takeWhile an infinite iterate/generate hangs the pipeline, and intermediate operations such as sorted(), distinct() or reduce buffer the whole sequence.
Parallel streams and generators mix badly: iterate/generate produce ordered, stateful sources that split poorly, and side effects in the lambdas become order-dependent races.

variants.name: Hand-written Iterator / Iterable (for-each protocol)
variants.idiom_name: Iterator<T> with hasNext()/next(); optionally a Spliterator for stream adaptation
variants.implementation_notes: Implement Iterator<T> (or Iterable<T> handing out a fresh iterator per call) when the producer owns state the stream API cannot express: a closeable resource, a checked exception, an early stop that must run cleanup, or a cursor the caller advances by hand. for-each drives it directly, StreamSupport.stream(Spliterators.spliteratorUnknownSize(...)) adapts it to pipelines, and a trySplit()-capable Spliterator is what makes the source parallelisable.
pitfalls: next() must be safe to call with or without hasNext() and must throw NoSuchElementException at the end: using that exception as control flow in production loops is a bug, not a contract.
A cursor is shared mutable state: it cannot be replayed or iterated by two consumers, and it is not thread-safe; split the roles (Iterable returns a fresh Iterator) instead of caching one iterator.
